Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 4:12: And on the night following the fast, he should be careful not to fill his belly with meat and wine, in a manner that would make his heart proud, so that his reward not go out in his loss - and the penitent must distance himself from these, especially from wine, as they said in the Zohar (Parashat Miketz, page 202a): what is said, that a person should remember that day of death - certainly it is so, because it breaks a person's heart, for the evil inclination rests only in a place where the joy of wine and the haughtiness of spirit are found, and when it finds a broken spirit, it then separates from him and does not rest with him - to this point. And since he says "haughtiness of spirit," one must distance himself from pleasures in a manner that his spirit not come to be proud over him.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 4:13: And many Torah scholars in our generation rely on not fasting, from what we say (Ta'anit 11a): Shmuel said, whoever sits in a fast is called a sinner - he held like this Tanna, who taught: Rabbi Elazar HaKappar the son of Rabbi says, what does Scripture teach by saying (Numbers 6:11), "and he shall atone for him, for that he sinned by reason of the soul"? Against what soul did this one sin? Rather, it is because he afflicted himself by abstaining from wine - and by an a fortiori argument: if this one, who only afflicted himself by abstaining from wine, is called a sinner, how much more so one who afflicts himself from everything! Rabbi Elazar says, he is called holy, as it is said (ibid. 6:5), "he shall be holy, he shall let the locks of the hair of his head grow" - and if this one, who only afflicted himself in one thing, is called holy, how much more so one who afflicts himself from everything! And according to Shmuel, is this one really called holy? Rather, that one who purifies his soul. And according to Rabbi Elazar, is this one really called a sinner? Rather, that one who defiles his soul. And did Rabbi Elazar really say this? Did not Rabbi Elazar say, a person should always regard himself as though a holy one dwelt within his innards, as it is said (Hosea 11:9), "the Holy One is in your midst, and I will not enter the city"? This is not difficult - one case is where he can afflict his soul [without harm], and the other is where he cannot afflict his soul. Reish Lakish said, he is called pious, as it is said (Proverbs 11:17), "a man of kindness rewards his own soul." Rav Sheshet said, this student of the House of Study who sits in a fast, let a dog eat his portion [i.e., it's worthless]. Rabbi Yirmiyah bar Abba said, there is no communal fast in Babylonia except the Ninth of Av alone. Rabbi Yirmiyah bar Abba said in the name of Reish Lakish, a Torah scholar is not permitted to sit in a fast, because it diminishes the work of Heaven - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 4:14: And from this final statement of Reish Lakish, they [Torah scholars] support themselves not to fast, and as Rashi, peace be upon him, explained - "because it diminishes the work of Heaven" - he becomes weak and cannot study - to this point. And since he is weak and cannot study, he is called "one who cannot afflict his soul," and is called a sinner. And the statement of Reish Lakish, who said he is called pious, as it is said, "a man of kindness rewards his own soul," must be reconciled, according to their view, as referring to one who can afflict his soul [without harm], or one who is not a Torah scholar - so that Reish Lakish not contradict himself, having said that a Torah scholar is not permitted to sit in a fast.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 4:15: And none of this supports one who has sinned not fasting, and that Torah should suffice for the atonement of his iniquity - for one who has sinned, even if he is a Torah scholar, his Torah is not acceptable until he purifies himself, as explained at the end of chapter 2 - and the proof of this is Reish Lakish himself, as explained in Pirkei D'Rabbi Eliezer (chapter 42), whose words we copied above (chapter 3), that after he repented, all his days he was occupied with fasting, charity, and prayer. Rather, certainly the words of Reish Lakish [about not fasting] are said only of a Torah scholar who has not sinned - for if he wishes to fast in order to sanctify himself, he is not permitted, because it diminishes the work of Heaven; but if he has sinned and sits in a fast, he is called pious, as it is said, "a man of kindness rewards his own soul" - and the explanation of "rewards his own soul" is that he rewards his soul, paying it according to its measure, as the verse says (Psalms 62:13), "and to You, O LORD, belongs kindness; for You render to a man according to his work" - behold, with the attribute of Chesed, a man is repaid according to his work. And so he explained that through accepting suffering, one brings himself near to Chesed, as he says (Proverbs 13:24), "but he who loves him disciplines him early" - and love is the love of Chesed, and unqualified purity is from the side of Chesed, as we explained above (chapter 3).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 4:16: And further we say in the Yerushalmi, in Nedarim, chapter Konam (chapter 8, halachah 1): Rabbi Yonatan would fast every eve of Rosh Hashanah; Rabbi Avin would fast every eve of Shabbat; Rabbi Ze'ira fasted three hundred fasts - some say nine hundred fasts - and paid no heed to Megillat Ta'anit - to this point. And so it is found in the Yerushalmi, Ta'anit, chapter 2 (halachah 12).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 4:17: And so the Tur wrote (Laws of Shabbat, section 249): one does not fix a meal on the eve of Shabbat, out of honor for Shabbat - and he wrote afterward: and it appears that it is the custom of men of [good] deeds to fast the whole day, as it is found in Eruvin (40b): "these students of the master who were sitting in a fast on the eve of Shabbat, what about completing it?" - this shows that it is the custom of Torah scholars to fast on the eve of Shabbat - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 4:18: Also, no proof should be brought from what we say in Ta'anit (22b): Rabbi Yosi says, an individual is not permitted to afflict himself with fasting, lest he become a burden on the community. For this is resolved by what the Ran, of blessed memory, wrote there: he already explained above that because they fast on these matters consecutively, he says that an individual is not permitted to fast on these matters consecutively. And the explanation of his words, that he said "because they fast on these matters consecutively" - the intent is, as it says there: our Rabbis taught, a city surrounded by marauding bands, or a river [in flood], or a ship tossed at sea, or an individual pursued by gentiles, or by an evil spirit, or by robbers - they sound the alarm even on Shabbat, but for all these an individual is not permitted to afflict himself with fasting, lest he become a burden on the community, and the community not have mercy on him. Behold, Rabbi Yosi is responding to the words of the first Tanna, concerning afflicting oneself with fasts for another - such as praying for a city surrounded by marauding bands, or for an individual being pursued - and as the Ran explained, that for these it is permitted to fast consecutively, and it is on these that Rabbi Yosi disagrees, saying that he should not fast consecutively because he will neglect his work, and so on - but concerning one who fasts consecutively for repentance for his own iniquities, Rabbi Yosi did not speak of this.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 4:19: And on the contrary, a good blessing shall come upon him - for in Tractate Yoma (86b), Mar Zutra bar Tuvya said in the name of Rav, great is repentance, for even if an individual does it, he is forgiven, and the whole world with him, as it is said (Hosea 14:5), "I will heal their backsliding." And not only that, but it brings healing to the world, as we say there (86a): Rabbi said, great is repentance, for it brings healing to the world, as it is said (Jeremiah 3:22), "return, backsliding children, I will heal your backslidings" - and if there is power in repentance to bring healing to the world, all the more so to himself, to bring healing so that he be healthy and not fall ill. And should you say that repentance is without fasting - the prophet has already explicitly stated the conditions of repentance (Joel 2:12), "with all your heart, with fasting, and with weeping, and with mourning."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 4:20: And further they said in Midrash Mishlei on the verse (Proverbs 6:4), "give no sleep to your eyes" - in these words: give no sleep to your eyes from occupying yourself with Torah, which atones for iniquity. Another interpretation: give no sleep to your eyes from performing repentance, for repentance and good deeds are a shield against punishment. Another interpretation: give no sleep to your eyes from sitting in a fast, for the fast is close to repentance, as it is said (Joel 2:12-13), "and rend your heart, and not your garments, and return to the LORD your God; if you do so, for He is gracious and merciful" - and why all this? In order to be saved from the judgment of Gehinnom - and concerning them it is explicit in the Tradition (Proverbs 6:5), "deliver yourself as a gazelle from the hand, and as a bird from the hand of the fowler" - so that you not be caught in the descent into Gehinnom. Another interpretation: "and as a bird from the hand of the fowler" - that you not become straw for the fire of Gehinnom - because the power of repentance reaches up to the Throne of Glory - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 4:21: Behold, he said that the fast is close to repentance, and the reason is as explained above at the beginning of the chapter. And therefore we find that for every distress that may come upon the community, a fast is decreed, as we learn in the first chapter of Ta'anit (chapter 1, mishnah 4): if the seventeenth of Cheshvan arrived and rain had not fallen, individuals would begin to fast. And why should they fast? Would it not be better that they occupy themselves with Torah, which atones for iniquity, and examine their deeds without a fast? Rather, the fast is necessary in order to bring about humbling - and when one is sanctified from eating and drinking, which are the powers of the body, he cleaves to Him, blessed be He, and to His ministers, who are separated and holy from eating and drinking, and then He answers us because we are cleaved to Him; but through eating and drinking we are separated from Him - except when eating is itself a commandment, on Shabbat, festivals, New Moons, and the like.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 4:22: And it is possible that for this reason Mar the son of Ravina would sit in a fast the whole year, as we say in Pesachim (68b): Mar the son of Ravina would sit in a fast the entire year, except for Shavuot, Purim, and the eve of the Day of Atonement.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 4:23: And one who cannot fast the entire year consecutively should at least strive to fulfill the words of Rabbi Yaakov, author of the Turim (Orach Chaim, section 580), in these words: it is written in Halachot Gedolot: these are the days on which one fasts by Torah law, and one who fasts on them shall neither eat nor drink until evening - on the first of Nisan, the sons of Aaron died, and so on - and he wrote at the end of his words: these are the days of fasting Israel received from the Torah, and further they decreed that they fast for three reasons - Monday and Thursday and Monday - over the destruction of the Temple, over the Torah that was burned, and over the disgrace of the Name; and in the future, the Holy One, blessed be He, will turn them into gladness and joy - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 4:24: And so they said in Masechet Soferim, that the students fast on the second and fifth days [Monday and Thursday] of Nisan, and the reason is because it is our Rabbis' decree over the three matters mentioned. In these words, in the last chapter, halachah 3: therefore they do not say supplications throughout the days of Nisan, and they do not fast until Nisan has passed - except the firstborns, who fast on the eve of Passover, and the pious, for the sake of the matzah, so that they enter it with appetite; and the students fast on Monday and Thursday during it, because of the profanation of the Name and out of honor for the Sanctuary that was burned - this applies in private, but to mention it in public is forbidden until Nisan has passed - to this point. Behold, that it was permitted for students to fast on Monday and Thursday during Nisan, because of the profanation of the Name, and the reason is that since it is their custom to fast this way the whole year, it teaches us that they do not stop during Nisan.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 4:25: And they wrote in the Tosafot (Bava Kamma 82a, s.v. "kedei"), concerning what we say, that Ezra instituted that the Torah be read on Monday and Thursday, so that they not go three days without Torah - and should you ask, why specifically Monday and Thursday? One may say, because it is said in the Midrash that Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, ascended on Thursday to receive the second tablets, and descended on Monday, and the Omnipresent was reconciled with him - and since it was a time of favor at that ascent and descent, they fixed [the Torah reading] on Monday and Thursday, and therefore they also became accustomed to fast on Monday and Thursday - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 4:26: And besides Monday and Thursday, there are days on which Israel has become accustomed to fast. On the eve of the New Moon they became accustomed to fast, and they say it is a "small Yom Kippur" - and the reason for this fast's existence is that Israel counts by the moon, as explained in the Zohar (Parashat Vayechi, beginning of pages 236b-237a), because this moon alludes to the supernal moon, and just as there is diminishment and lack below, so above - and the righteous, who suffer the sufferings of the Shechinah, accept the judgment that comes upon them, and just as she is renewed, so are they renewed with her.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 4:27: And so they said in the Zohar (Parashat Vayeshev, page 181a), concerning the righteous who have suffering because they were born at the moon's diminishment - that in the future they have a great virtue, and the Shechinah does not move from them - in these words there: and when the moon is blemished on that side of the evil serpent, then all those souls that go out - even though they are all pure and all holy, since they went out at the time of diminishment - in all those places those souls reach, they are all broken and blemished with several sorrows and several pains; and these are the souls in the places the Holy One, blessed be He, delights in, after they have been broken - and even though souls are in sadness and not in gladness, the secret of the matter is that it rests in the manner of what is above: the body is blemished and the soul within, in the manner of what is above - certainly in this manner. And therefore these are the ones who wish to be renewed with the renewal of the moon, and of them it is written (Isaiah 66:23), "and it shall come to pass, that from one New Moon to another, and from one Sabbath to another, shall all flesh come to worship before Me, says the LORD" - "all flesh" certainly, for these shall be renewed in everything, and wish to be renewed with the renewal of the moon, and these are partnered together with the moon, blemished with her blemish - and therefore she rests among them always, not abandoning them, along the lines of (Isaiah 57:15), "and with him who is of a contrite and humble spirit," and it is written (Psalms 34:19), "the LORD is near to the brokenhearted" - to those who suffered with the moon that blemish, they are always near to her - and therefore, "to revive the heart of the contrite ones" - with that life that comes to her to be renewed, their portion shall be; those who suffered with her shall be renewed with her - and these are called "sufferings of love" - "of love" they are, and not from the person himself - "of love" they are, for the light of the "small love" is blemished, which is pushed away from the "great love" - and therefore these are companions partnered with her, happy is their portion in this world and in the World to Come, for they have merited this, to be companions with her - of them it is written (Psalms 122:8), "for the sake of my brothers and companions," and so on - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 4:28: And from here we learn that whoever suffers with the suffering of the Shechinah has a great reward, as explained in the discourse, that "the LORD is near to the brokenhearted, to those who suffered with the moon that blemish," and so on - it appears that everyone who humbles himself with suffering and breaks his heart is renewed with her. And therefore, on the eve of the New Moon, when she is entirely blemished, it is fitting to suffer and fast. And on every fast one undertakes, it is good that he intend this too - besides that, through his sin, he caused her affliction, as we elaborated in the Gate of Fear, that "a foolish son is the grief of his mother" - therefore it is fitting that he suffer affliction in place of the affliction he caused her, all the more so now in this exile of ours, for "because of our transgressions our mother was sent away" - it is fitting for every person to suffer with her suffering, and to accept suffering for prolonging the exile through our iniquities - and concerning the matter of humility we elaborated further - see there.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 4:29: Further, there are days on which Israel has become accustomed to fast, such as from the New Moon of Elul until the Day of Atonement, which are days on which Selichot and supplications are said - and they relied for this on (Song of Songs 6:3), "*I am my beloved's, *and my beloved is mine" - initial letters spell "Elul," and the final letters are four yuds, corresponding to forty days; and so (Deuteronomy 30:6), "and the LORD your God will circumcise *your heart, *and the heart of" - initial letters spell "Elul" - for this month is prepared for the circumcision of the heart, namely repentance.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 4:30: And it stands to reason, since it is the last month of the year, to perform repentance in it for what one has blemished the whole year, and not enter Rosh Hashanah, which is the day of judgment, defiled by his evil deeds - but rather to repair in this month what has passed. And so too the Ten Days of Repentance - their very name proves that they were established for the repair of the year, and they are days of judgment in which we say "the King of judgment," and the Holy One, blessed be He, is ready to receive penitents then, as they expounded, of blessed memory, "seek the LORD while He may be found" (Isaiah 55:6) - are there days when He is not found? Rather, this refers to an individual, and so on - that on these days, even an individual is found - and it is fitting to fast and examine his deeds and fulfill the essentials of repentance with all his heart, in fasting and weeping and mourning, and at night not eat meat nor drink wine.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 4:31: And Rabbenu Yonah wrote in Sha'arei Teshuvah (Gate 2, letter 14), in these words: during the Ten Days of Repentance, one who fears the word of the LORD, his heart shall trembel within him, knowing that all his deeds are written in a book, and at that time God will bring every deed into judgment, over everything hidden, whether good or evil - for a person is judged on Rosh Hashanah, and his sentence is sealed on the Day of Atonement. And when a person knows that his case will be brought before a king of flesh and blood, will he not tremble greatly and take counsel with his soul, and by every diligent means hasten his own rescue, and it would not enter his mind to turn right or left and occupy himself with his other affairs? Therefore, how foolish are those who go out to their work and their labor until evening during these awesome days, the days of judgment and verdict, not knowing what their judgment will be! And it is fitting for every God-fearing person to reduce his affairs and keep his thoughts sealed, and to set times, day and night, to seclude himself in his chambers, to examine his ways and investigate, and to rise before the watches to occupy himself with the ways of repentance and worthy deeds, and to pour out his meditation and lift up prayer and joyous song and cast down supplication - for the time is a time of favor, and prayer is heard in it. And our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said, "seek the LORD while He may be found" - these are the ten days between Rosh Hashanah and the Day of Atonement.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 4:32: And it is a positive commandment of the Torah that a person arouse his spirit and return in repentance on the Day of Atonement, as it is said (Leviticus 16:30), "from all your sins before the LORD you shall be pure" - and our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said that the Day of Atonement atones together with repentance; therefore Scripture warned us to purify ourselves before the LORD through our repentance, and He shall atone for us on this day, to purify us - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 4:33: And when the discerning one considers the accounts mentioned in the Gemara of sages who fasted so many fasts, and sees that the matter was, so it seems, without such great necessity, his soul will be inflamed to fast for all his iniquities - and each person knows the iniquities that have preceded him.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 4:34: The Rosh wrote in the "Small Halachot" of Rabbi Yitzchak Alfasi (page 8a), concerning what we say (Menachot 35b): Rav Ashi was sitting before Mar Zutra when his tefillin strap became flipped - in these words, a Gaon's responsum: concerning Rav Huna's strap, which was flipped and he sat forty days in a fast - whether it was of the hand-tefillin or the head-tefillin - thus we have learned from our masters, that it was the head-tefillin; Rav Huna who sat in a fast, it was not because it was an obligation, and so on. And this incident of Rav Huna is brought in the Gemara of Tractate Mo'ed Katan (25a). And he wrote another responsum: one who flips the strap of the head-tefillin or the hand-tefillin is obligated to sit in a fast, for he is negligent and requires a fast - but to obligate him to forty fasts like Rav Huna, no - and it was out of abundant piety that he did so - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 4:35: And so we find that Rabbi Ze'ira fasted a hundred fasts so that the fire of Gehinnom not rule over him, as is found in the Gemara (Bava Metzia 85a), besides two hundred others he fasted, as explained there. Also in the Yerushalmi (Shabbat, chapter 5, halachah 4), concerning what we say, that Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah's cow would go out with a strap, and so on - our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said: Rabbi Chanina said, once it went out and its teeth had blackened from the fasts - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 4:36: Also, if a Torah scholar fasts so that Torah endure in him and not cease from his descendants, it is good for him - as is found there, in "One Who Hires Workers" (85a), concerning what we say: Rabbi Parnach said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan, whoever is a Torah scholar, and his son a Torah scholar, and his son's son a Torah scholar, Torah will never again cease from his descendants, as it is said (Isaiah 59:21), "and I, this is My covenant with them," and so on. Rav Yosef sat forty fasts, and they read to him [the words], "shall not depart from your mouth" - and he sat forty more fasts, and they read to him, "nor from the mouth of your seed" - he sat a hundred more fasts, and they read to him, "shall not depart from your mouth, nor from the mouth of your seed, nor from the mouth of your seed's seed." He said, from now on I need no more - Torah returns to its own lodging - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 4:37: And so we find that Solomon fasted forty fasts for wisdom, as is found at the beginning of Midrash Mishlei, concerning the reason the Book of Proverbs begins with a mem.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 4:38: And in the secret of the fast, they explained in the Zohar (Parashat Shemot, pages 20a-b); he says there, on the verse (Song of Songs 2:16), "my beloved is mine, and I am his, who feeds among the lilies" - that the Holy One, blessed be He, conducts His world with kindness and judgment, alluded to by the lilies, which have red and white in them, in these words: what is this lily, red and white? So the fragrance of the sacrifice is from red and white. Come and see, from the fragrance of the incense - some of the spices are white, some are red, such as frankincense, which is white, and myrrh, which is red - and the fragrance rises from red and white; and therefore He conducts His world like lilies, which are red and white, as it is written (Ezekiel 44:15), "to offer Me the fat and the blood." Corresponding to this, a person offers his fat and his blood, and is atoned for - this is red and this is white. Just as this lily, red and white, cannot be reduced to become entirely white except through fire, so a sacrifice cannot be reduced to become entirely white except through fire. Now, whoever sits in his fast and offers up his fat and his blood is not reduced to be entirely white except through fire, for Rabbi Yehuda said, through a person's fast his limbs are weakened and the fire prevails over him, and at that hour he must offer his fat and his blood in that fire, and this is called an altar of atonement. And this is what Rabbi Elazar said, when he would sit and pray, saying: it is revealed and known before You, LORD my God and God of my fathers, that I have offered before You my fat and my blood, and boiled them with the heat of my body's weakness - may it be Your will before You that the fragrance rising from my mouth at this hour be like the fragrance rising from the sacrifice in the fire of the altar, and that You be reconciled with me. It follows that a person who offers, in his fast, the fat, the blood, and the fire, and the fragrance that rises, is an altar of atonement. And therefore they instituted prayer in place of the sacrifice, provided he intends what we have said. Rabbi Yitzchak said, from here onward it is written (Numbers 31:23), "every thing that may abide the fire, you shall make it go through the fire, and it shall be pure" - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 4:39: Further, he should intend what they said in the Zohar, Parashat Terumah (page 153a): there are three rulers above through whom the Holy One, blessed be He, is known, and they are His precious secret - these are the brain, the heart, and the liver, and they are in the reverse order of this world. Above, the brain takes first, and afterward gives to the heart, and the heart takes and gives to the liver, and afterward the liver gives a portion to all those sources below, each and every one as is fitting for it. Below, the liver takes first, and afterward it brings everything near to the heart, and the heart takes it - once the heart has taken it and been strengthened by that strength and will that it takes, it arouses toward the brain, and afterward the liver returns and distributes food to all the limbs of the body. On the day of a fast, a person brings his food and drink near to the supernal liver, brings near his fat, his blood, and his will - that liver takes everything with will; once everything is with it, it takes it and offers everything to the heart, which is greater and rules over it; once the heart takes it and is strengthened with will, it brings everything near to the brain, which is the supernal ruler over the whole body; afterward the liver returns and distributes portions to all those sources and limbs below - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 4:40: And one who contemplates the words of this discourse will see, with the eye of understanding, that the fast is literally a sacrifice, the secret of "an offering made by fire, a sweet savor to the LORD" (Leviticus 1:9), which they explained in the Zohar on Song of Songs. And therefore one must be careful, on the day of the fast, of every sin and iniquity, so that his sacrifice not be rejected - and he should discern from the things that disqualify a sacrifice, one of which is [wrongful] thought - and so too they disqualify a fast, if he contemplates a transgression. And so the other things that disqualify a sacrifice disqualify a fast - and therefore he must abandon sin, not being one who immerses while holding a creeping thing in his hand.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 4:41: And in Tractate Berachot (32b), concerning the fast, they said, of blessed memory: and Rabbi Elazar said, fasting is greater than charity - what is the reason? This one is with his body, and that one is with his money - to this point. And he said "fasting is greater," and so on, teaching us thereby the virtue of charity - for one thing is not called greater than another unless they belong to the same category and standard - and the reason is that charity atones for iniquity, as he says (Daniel 4:24), "and break off your sin by righteousness," and likewise the fast is in place of the sacrifice and atones for iniquity, as they said there, chapter "Hayah Korei" (Berachot 17a): Rav Sheshet, when he would sit in a fast, after praying would say this: Master of the universe, it is revealed before You that at the time the Temple stood, a person would sin and offer a sacrifice, and only his fat and blood were offered from it, and he was atoned for - and now I have sat in a fast and my fat and blood have diminished; may it be Your will before You that my fat and blood that have diminished be as though I offered them before You upon the altar, and that You be reconciled with me - to this point. And fasting adds to charity in that it is with his body, for he offers up his own countenance above - and just as, at the time the Temple stood, in the performance of the sacrifice, the essence of the sacrifice was humbling, so they said in the Zohar (Parashat Pinchas, page 240b): the beginning of the sacrifice is at the hour a person confesses his sins over it, and its slaughtering and the sprinkling of its blood on the altar - to this point. Further, on page 241a: Adam is engraved on the throne; Adam is the essence of everything, and he offers there his spirit and his soul - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 4:42: And it says in the Yerushalmi, chapter Keitzad (Ta'anit, chapter 2, halachah 1), in these words: Rabbi Abba bar Zavda expounded, "let us lift up our heart with our hands" (Lamentations 3:41) - and is it possible for a person to take his heart and put it in his hand? Rather, what is "lift up"? Let us make our hearts like the palms of our hands - and afterward, "to God in the heavens." So, if there is a creeping thing in a person's hand, even if he immerses in the waters of Shiloach or the waters of creation, he has no eternal purity; but if he casts it from his hand, he is immediately pure - to this point. And the intent is that just as the hands must have no creeping thing in them, namely iniquity, so too the heart must be like the palms, clean of contemplating the performance of a transgression, as it is said (Isaiah 55:7), "let the wicked forsake his way, and the man of iniquity his thoughts" - and "nissa" [lift up] is a term of equalizing, like "nishavi" [we shall make equal].
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 4:43: Also, the essence of the fast, especially a communal fast, must involve the examination of one's deeds, as it is said (Lamentations 3:40), "let us search and examine our ways, and turn back to the LORD" - it appears that there is no way to the repentance stated as "return, O Israel, to the LORD," except through investigation and examination of one's deeds. And this is the essence of the fast, as the prophet Isaiah, peace be upon him, said (Isaiah 58:3), in what he says there: "why have we fasted, and You do not see? Why have we afflicted our soul, and You do not notice?" and so on - and afterward he says, "is such the fast that I have chosen? A day for a man to afflict his soul? Is it to bow down his head like a bulrush, and to spread sackcloth and ashes under him? Will you call this a fast, and an acceptable day to the LORD? Is not this the fast that I have chosen: to loose the bonds of wickedness, to undo the bands of the yoke?" And the first verse he said, "is such the fast that I have chosen," and so on, "a day of afflicting," and so on, "to bow down like a bulrush," and so on, is in the form of a rhetorical question - meaning, that none of this is desired before Him; but the chosen fast is "to loose the bonds of wickedness."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 4:44: And so they explained in the Yerushalmi, Ta'anit, chapter 2 (halachah 1), in these words: Rabbi Elazar said, "is such the fast that I have chosen" - rather, "a day for a man to afflict his soul" - this is not a fast I desire; and what fast do I desire? "Is not this the fast that I have chosen: to loose the bonds of wickedness, to undo the bands of the yoke; is it not to share your bread with the hungry, and bring the wandering poor into your house?" What is written after it? "Then shall you call, and the LORD shall answer," and so on - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 4:45: It follows that the sum of the fast requires the examination of one's deeds, the abandonment of sin, and giving charity for its own sake, as is explained in the verse, which contains several aspects one must scrutinize in the verse, all of which relate to the matter of charity.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 4:46: And so they explained in Tractate Ta'anit (12b), concerning what is written about Ezra, when he decreed a fast upon them (Nehemiah 9:3), "and they read in the book of the Torah of God a fourth part of the day," and so on, in these words: Abaye said, on a fast day, from morning until midday they examine matters of the city, and from midday, a quarter of the day they read and take leave [of study for prayer], and a quarter of the day they seek mercy - as it is said, "and they read in the book of the Torah of God a fourth part of the day, and a fourth part they confessed and worshipped." And I would reverse it - no, this cannot be, for it is written, "and to me were gathered all who trembled" [implying that seeking mercy came after examining matters] - to this point. Behold, that the first half of the day is spent in examining one's deeds, before Torah and prayer.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 4:47: And so they explained in the Zohar (Parashat Vayechi, page 228b), on the verse (Isaiah 38:2), "then Chizkiyahu turned his face to the wall" - that one should not pray about a sin until he has directed all his intent to repairing his iniquity, in these words, in brief: from here we learn that whoever has an iniquity and wishes to seek mercy concerning it should direct his face and his thoughts to repairing himself from that iniquity, and afterward seek his prayer - along the lines of (Lamentations 3:40), "let us search and examine our ways, and let us turn back to the LORD" - "let us search our ways" first, and afterward, "and let us turn back" - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 4:48: And concerning the matter of charity, they said in Sanhedrin (35a): Rabbi Elazar said, any fast in which charity is delayed [in being distributed] overnight is as though [the community] shed blood, as it is said (Isaiah 1:21), "righteousness lodged in her, but now murderers" - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 4:49: And in Sefer Chassidim (section 226) it is written: know and understand, although the Sages said a fast is as good for a [bad] dream as fire for tow, they said this only for those who do repentance along with the fast. Behold, a certain Jew saw [a bad dream] in a dream on the night of the ninth of Tishrei, and fasted on the ninth and on the Day of Atonement - behold, two days and a night - and it did not help him, because they show him a harsh dream so that he examine his deeds, for the fast is in place of a sin-offering - just as a sacrifice does not avail without repentance, as it is said (Proverbs 21:27), "the sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination," so a fast for a dream does not avail without repentance - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 4:50: And Rabbenu Tam wrote in Sefer HaYashar that on the day of the fast one must be careful of anger, because the bile grows stronger. And so he also wrote in Sefer Chassidim (section 617): when a person fasts, he should guard himself from being irritable that day, for when a person is hungry he is irritable - and if he will become angry, it would be better for him not to fast, and to be satisfied and of good disposition toward people, so as not to quarrel - and it is written (Isaiah 58:4), "behold, you fast for strife and contention, and to strike with the fist of wickedness; you shall not fast as you do this day," and so on. And the ancients, when they fasted, would eat only bread with salt and drink water - like Rabbi Yehoshua, who spoke against Beit Shammai (Chagigah 22b) - to this point.
